Meeting header:

Attendees: Laura (Redwood AE), Marco (Redwood SE), Samir (CTO), Jules (Head of ML), Ava (Infra)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Vireo is evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployment modes focused on unit economics. They care about per-token cost, latency SLOs for customer-facing assistants, and annual budget constraints (target ~$120k/year for inference). Discussed batching, prefix/KV cache, quantization tradeoffs, and potential dedicated reserved capacity to meet predictable throughput. Agreed to share pricing worksheet, security docs, and schedule a performance pilot.

Topics: cost per token math; batching & caching levers; dedicated reserved capacity vs burst; private deployment network/KMS; success criteria and timeline.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Laura: Okay hi everyone, thanks for joining — I think we have about 40 minutes. Quick intros?
[00:06] Samir: Samir here, CTO at Vireo, overseeing infra and product. Jules runs the models and evaluation, Ava is our infra lead.
[00:11] Jules: Hi all.
[00:12] Ava: Hey.
[00:13] Laura: Great. Marco with Redwood here — SE who will dig into perf and batching.
[00:18] Marco: Hey folks.
[00:20] Laura: High level — Vireo reached out asking about how we think about per-token costs and tradeoffs between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. The goal for today is to understand your traffic profile and budget so we can recommend a path (pilot vs dedicated commit).
[00:33] Samir: Yeah, we have a couple threads. One is cost — we have a hard constraint, roughly $10k/month targeted for inference initially, scaling up. Second is latency for our consumer assistant, we need 300-400ms 95th p90? — something like that. Third is data controls, since some customers tag data as sensitive, so VPC or private might be needed for certain tenants.
[00:52] Jules: Also curious about batching and cache savings. Our prompts are typically multi-turn, lots of repeated system prompts, and for a single session we expect maybe on average 200 tokens/request and 1.2 requests/session.
[01:06] Laura: Great, that gives us some starting numbers. Quick clarifying question: when you say 200 tokens/request, is that total input+output or just the generation portion?
[01:14] Jules: total tokens including response generation — about 50 tokens are output on average, 150 tokens input.
[01:20] Marco: Helpful — we typically price/measure per output token but do account for input tokens for quota. For Hosted customers, we show combined token counts in billing.
[01:30] Samir: Can you walk through a back-of-envelope? If we do Hosted and assume X per-1k tokens, how does that scale to our $10k/month?
[01:38] Laura: Sure — wild example numbers for illustration. If per-token equivalent is $0.0003 per token (i.e., $0.30 per 1k tokens), then 1M tokens/day is roughly $300/day or ~$9k/month. But that is naive because you can lower cost with batching and caching and also move to Dedicated where reserved capacity brings unit cost down.
[02:02] Jules: That rough calc is helpful. Our expected traffic is about 200k requests/day, if average tokens/request is 200 that's 40M tokens/day which is way more than those numbers — so we'd be at $12k/day at that naive rate which is no go. So we need optimizations.
[02:21] Ava: Right our real traffic has a heavy head of short queries — many are 20 token asks, some long context retrievals. We have session reuse — same prompt templates — so caching might help.
[02:33] Marco: This is exactly where batching and prefix/KV caching matter. Two levers: 1) batching — increasing tokens-per-invocation by grouping concurrent requests reduces per-token overhead; 2) prefix and KV cache — if your system frequently reuses the same context (system prompts or few-shot examples), caching can avoid recomputing attended states. Both can reduce cost dramatically, sometimes 2-7x depending on request shape.
[02:58] Samir: Can you explain the math for batching? Like how does batching interact with latency SLOs?
[03:03] Marco: Sure — if you batch N concurrent requests, GPU throughput across those requests is amortized. But batching introduces queueing latency — so you need to tune max_batch_size and max_wait_ms. For a user-facing 300-400ms 95th, acceptable batching windows are small; maybe 10-30ms wait is okay, but if you batch for 100ms you'll violate latency for interactive flows. For non-interactive backfills you can batch much more aggressively.
[03:28] Jules: Do you support hybrid policies, like low-latency pool for interactive and high-throughput pool for background jobs?
[03:33] Marco: Yes — Smart routing lets you route by policy: latency-sensitive requests bound to a low-latency pool (maybe with smaller batch sizes and higher cost), and background jobs to a bulk pool (larger batches, lower cost). Hosted and Dedicated both support routing; in private deployments you can orchestrate similar pools.
[03:49] Ava: About cache — you said KV cache and prefix cache. Our engineers call it K V cache sometimes; what's the reliability of that? Is it per worker? Sticky session?
[03:58] Marco: KV cache is per model instance — it's the cached key/value tensors for attention allowing we to avoid recomputing for prefixes. For chat with long histories, KV cache saves repeated compute for the prior tokens. It is sticky to an invocation but can be used across user sessions if you use our prefix cache feature which stores compiled prefix states and can be reattached. In Hosted we manage invalidation; in Private you control retention. There are tradeoffs for memory.
[04:23] Samir: So if we have 70% of requests that share the same system prompt, could that be a 2-3x cost reduction?
[04:28] Marco: Yes, in that ballpark. With identical prefixes and our prefix cache you avoid re-encoding the prefix each time. Real-world savings depend on model and how much of total token work is prefix vs generation.
[04:40] Laura: Quick interruption — I want to make sure we map this to dollars. Marco, can you run a micro-scenario: say 200k requests/day, median tokens/request 60 (after we optimize), 50% cache hit rate for prefix, plus batching efficiency of 1.8x. What's the rough cost delta between Hosted naive and optimized?
[04:57] Marco: Okay. Naive: 200k * 60 = 12M tokens/day. At $0.30 per 1k tokens -> $3.6k/day -> $108k/month. With 50% prefix cache hit, effective tokens dropped to 6M/day. With batching giving 1.8x improvement, compute equivalent is ~3.33M tokens/day. That's ~$1k/day or $30k/month. Then if you move to Dedicated reserved capacity you might cut unit cost further by 20-30% depending on commit. So that gets closer to your $10k/month target but probably still above. These are illustrative.
[05:38] Samir: That clarifies. The critical unknowns are real-world cache hit rates and achievable batching because our traffic is spiky. We have daily peaks and sudden marketing-driven bursts.
[05:48] Ava: On spikes we need graceful degradation — ability to fallback to a cheaper model variant or region. How do you handle that?
[05:54] Marco: We have automated fallback policies — routing to compatible model variants or burst capacity across regions. For Hosted we can failover to a lower-cost variant and maintain response albeit lower quality. For Dedicated you can configure burst capacity and we can autoscale within preset SLOs. Private deployments need customer-managed autoscaling unless you opt for Redwood-managed private.
[06:13] Jules: For Private, what about encryption and KMS integrations? We have strict controls; some tenants demand HSM-backed keys and audit logs.
[06:20] Laura: We support KMS/HSM integrations and per-tenant audit logs in Private. We'll share the security docs.
[06:25] Samir: Timeline-wise — we're evaluating over the next quarter, want to decide whether to run a small pilot (Hosted) or aim for Dedicated reserved capacity. What's the recommended path?
[06:33] Marco: Typically we recommend a 4–6 week pilot on Hosted with production-ish traffic to validate caching hit rates and batching savings. If the model fits and costs scale predictably, you move to Dedicated commits to lower unit cost. If data residency or security is a blocker, consider Private early but that adds setup time.
[06:51] Ava: Setup time for Private — ballpark?
[06:54] Laura: With our on-prem or VPC private offering, from signed order to green can vary 6–12 weeks depending on network readiness and KMS. If you do VPC with cloud partner, often 4–8 weeks.
[07:06] Samir: Okay we may need Private for top tier customers but pilot Hosted first. We want tooling to simulate our traffic. Can you run synthetic load tests that match our request distribution?
[07:15] Marco: Yes, we have a perf harness and we'll parameterize by request size distribution, concurrency, and stubborn tails. We'll work with Ava for realistic keys and network setup.
[07:24] Jules: A quick question on quantization — can you support int8 or LLM-int8 for production? We try to trade off some quality for cost savings.
[07:31] Marco: We support several quantization profiles depending on model family; some give 2-4x speedups with minimal quality loss. We'll include our quantization recommendation in the cost model we send.
[07:41] Samir: And how do you measure quality regressions? We have a small eval suite with prompt sets — do you integrate that?
[07:47] Marco: Redwood Optimize integrates quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to eval sets. We can run your evals pre/post quant and measure metrics like F1, answer rate, or custom thresholds.
[07:56] Ava: For procurement, what does a Dedicated contract look like? Term lengths, commit levels?
[08:00] Laura: Typical Dedicated is a 12-month commit with monthly billing. Commit size and discounts scale with the annual spend. We can do monthly reserved tiers for early pilots. There's also a burst bucket for short spikes.
[08:12] Samir: If we do 12-month commit, what's the penalty for under-using reserved capacity?
[08:16] Laura: There are standard terms — unused committed capacity can sometimes roll into next period for a window, or you can renegotiate. We can share contract playbook.
[08:25] Jules: On measurement — we'd like token-level / route-level cost breakdown to map product features to spend. Does your Console show that?
[08:31] Marco: Yes, Console has token-level cost and latency breakdown by route, model, and token type. You can filter to tenant or API key to attribute spend.
[08:39] Samir: Good. For pilot we'll need an example dashboard.
[08:42] Laura: We'll share screenshots and a trial account config.
[08:46] 
[08:47] Noise / crosstalk for a minute while they share a doc link
[09:05] Jules: One operational detail — when a user resumes a long session, do you recommend reusing the same worker to keep KV cache warm? How sticky is that?
[09:12] Marco: Stickiness helps but isn't always guaranteed. We usually recommend prefix cache that persists compiled state independent of worker to get deterministic hits across invocations. Sticky sessions help with microsecond gains but prefix store gives broader bang-for-buck.
[09:27] Ava: About metrics we can provide — we will export a week's worth of logs with tokens per request, latency, and concurrency. Is that useful?
[09:35] Marco: Extremely. That will let us run offline simulations to estimate batch efficiency and cache hit rates.
[09:40] Samir: Are there any hidden cost buckets? GPU hours, request overhead, storage for caches?
[09:46] Marco: Good question. Billing is primarily token and optional Reserved capacity fees for Dedicated. There can be ancillary charges for high retention observability, private deployment support fees, and data egress depending on deployment. We will call those out in the pricing worksheet.
[10:02] Laura: Let's talk success criteria — what would make this project a win in 90 days?
[10:06] Jules: For ML, win is us proving a 2–3x reduction in inference unit cost with acceptable quality (less than 5% drop on our eval), and peak p95 latency under 500ms for interactive flows.
[10:17] Ava: For infra, win is a predictable monthly spend forecast plus clear autoscaling rules for spikes.
[10:22] Samir: For execs, win is a path to bring inference spend under the product budget and a decision whether to do Dedicated reserve next quarter.
[10:30] Marco: Good, that maps to a Hosted pilot followed by a commit decision.
[10:34]

[10:44] Samir: One last nit — can you give a sample cost scenario that shows delta between no-cache hosted vs dedicated with 50% caching and quantization? Just so we can show execs a slide.
[10:53] Marco: I'll prepare a slide. Roughly: No-cache hosted might be 3–4x more than hosted+cache+batching. Dedicated with a commit and quantization could be 2–3x cheaper than naive hosted. I will quantify with your real numbers.
[11:07] Laura: Great. Any other questions?
[11:09] Jules: Not on my side.
[11:10] Ava: None.
[11:11] Samir: Thanks.
[11:12] Laura: Thanks everyone. We'll send next steps and calendar invites for the perf window.
